statement: In drug-checking samples brought to eight harm-reduction sites in Vancouver and Surrey between October 2018 and January 2020, benzodiazepine urine test strips (BTNX Rapid Response, made to detect urine metabolites of common benzodiazepines) read by site staff, compared with confirmatory laboratory tests on a convenience subset of 153 samples, partly chosen because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose, missed many of the newer benzodiazepines not sold as medicines (NPS benzodiazepines) and also gave false positives. The strips read positive in 15 of 24 samples that contained an NPS benzodiazepine (62.5%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 42.7–78.8%): in 7 of 8 when flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam was present, but in 8 of 16 when etizolam was the only one (50%). They also read positive in 20 of 129 samples in which no NPS benzodiazepine was found (15.5%; 10.3–22.7%), and what made those react was not reported. Infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), used beside the strips, found 2 of the 24. The strips detected the prescribed benzodiazepines alprazolam and temazepam in all six samples that held only these (Laing et al., 2021). In pure solutions, the same maker's benzodiazepine strip detected diazepam and alprazolam from 0.1 µg/mL and bromazolam and flubromazepam from 0.25 µg/mL, but did not react to etizolam at any concentration tried from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL (Sisco et al., 2024b). Only 159 of 1368 strip-tested samples had laboratory confirmation, the two confirmatory laboratories disagreed on 2 of 7 positive samples tested at both, etizolam is reported to dissolve poorly in water, and targeted laboratory methods may miss the newest compounds; none of the 24 samples was expected by the person to contain an NPS benzodiazepine, and 17 of them also contained fentanyl. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Often not. At one drug-checking service, benzodiazepine strips missed 9 of 24 samples that held a newer benzodiazepine, and half of the samples with etizolam alone. They also read positive in about 16 in 100 samples with none. In a laboratory, the same maker's strip never reacted to pure etizolam. Few samples were checked by a laboratory, and many were chosen after suspected overdoses.
population: Drug-checking samples brought to eight harm-reduction sites in Vancouver and Surrey, Canada (2018 to 2020), of which 153 had confirmatory laboratory results; benzodiazepines in water in a second laboratory
exposure: BTNX benzodiazepine urine test strips (oxazepam calibrator, cut-off 300 ng/mL) used on dissolved drug by site staff, alongside FTIR; the same maker's strip in pure solutions
comparator: Confirmatory laboratory testing (GC–MS, LC-MS or qNMR) for NPS benzodiazepines; known content of prepared solutions
outcome: Detection of NPS benzodiazepines (sensitivity), false positives, and detection of individual benzodiazepines in water
magnitude: Laing et al. (153 samples with point-of-care and confirmatory results; 6 with only typical benzodiazepines removed): strips 15/24 NPS-benzodiazepine samples positive (62.5%; Wilson 42.7–78.8%, editors' calculation), false-negative rate 37.5%; 20/129 negatives positive (15.5%; 10.3–22.7%), specificity 84.5% (editors' calculation); 87.5% (n = 8) with flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam; 50.0% (n = 16; 28.0–72.0%) with etizolam alone; FTIR 2/24 (false-negative rate 91.7%), false-positive rate 3.9%; either method 17/24 detected, 23 false positives. Sisco et al. (2024b): limits 0.1 µg/mL (diazepam, alprazolam) and 0.25 µg/mL (bromazolam, flubromazepam); etizolam negative from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL.

evidence.extracted: Strips detected benzodiazepines in 62.5% (15/24) of confirmed NPS-benzodiazepine samples: 87.5% (n = 8) when flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam was present and 50.0% (n = 16) when etizolam was the only benzodiazepine. Of 35 strip positives, 20 (57.1%) had no NPS benzodiazepine on confirmatory testing (false-positive rate 15.5%); of 118 strip negatives, 9 (7.6%) contained one (false-negative rate 37.5%). FTIR: of 7 positives, 5 had no NPS benzodiazepine (false-positive rate 3.9%); 22 of 146 FTIR negatives contained one (false-negative rate 91.7%); FTIR identified 2 etizolam samples that were negative on strips. Editors' calculation: 129 confirmed negatives (20 + 109 in Table 3); Wilson 95% CI 42.7–78.8% for 15/24 and 10.3–22.7% for 20/129; 8 of 16 etizolam-only samples (28.0–72.0%).

evidence.locator: Results › NPS benzodiazepines and opioids, 1st paragraph; Results › Point-of-care accuracy & error, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Of the 24 NPS-benzodiazepine-positive samples, 17 (printed as 70.1%) also contained an opioid, always fentanyl. Six of the 159 samples (3.8%) contained only typical benzodiazepines (alprazolam and temazepam), each detected by test strips, and were removed from the NPS analysis; the authors present the detection values on the assumption that the strips, not designed for NPS benzodiazepines, have some ability to detect them. With both methods combined, 23 of 40 positives had no NPS benzodiazepine (false-positive rate 17.8%) and 7 of 113 samples negative on both contained one (false-negative rate 29.2%).

evidence.locator: Abstract; Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 2–3); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Table 1 (p. 5)
evidence.extracted: Eight harm-reduction sites in Vancouver and Surrey, October 2018 to January 2020; samples checked by FTIR and BTNX benzodiazepine strips (oxazepam calibrator, cut-off 300 ng/ml, validated by the maker for 22 benzodiazepines in urine); a convenience subset (discarded, unclaimed or client-requested samples, or samples clinically suspicious for benzodiazepine overdose) went to confirmatory testing; 1368 samples had both point-of-care checks; of 7 NPS-benzodiazepine-positive samples sent to both laboratories, 5 were confirmed at both and 2 at one only. No NPS-benzodiazepine sample was expected by the person to be one; 15 were expected to be fentanyl and 5 alprazolam.

evidence.extracted: The authors note that benzodiazepine immunoassay strips are designed to test urine for metabolites of common benzodiazepines such as oxazepam and nordiazepam and may give false negatives with NPS benzodiazepines or diluted drug samples; that etizolam is reportedly not soluble in water; that the small subsamples may under- or over-estimate the error rates; and that targeted confirmatory assays may miss the newest compounds.

evidence.locator: Results and Discussion › Effect of Organic Solvents on Test Strip Response, 3rd paragraph (AM p. 5); Limit of Detection, 3rd paragraph (AM p. 6); Cross-Reactivity, 4th paragraph (AM pp. 7–8)
evidence.extracted: BTNX benzodiazepine strips in water: approximate limit of detection 0.1 µg/mL for diazepam and alprazolam and 0.25 µg/mL for bromazolam and flubromazepam; etizolam gave no positive at either panel concentration or at several others between 0.01 and 0.5 mg/mL; MDMA, amphetamine and metamizole gave faint results at the high concentration; acetonitrile, a laboratory solvent, at more than about 10% v/v made the strips read negative when a positive was expected.

risk_of_bias.note: Laing et al. compares strips with confirmatory tests inside programme data (cross-sectional, JBI-prevalence high on the card) and is treated as accuracy evidence with high risk of bias: only 159 of 1368 point-of-care-tested samples were verified, chosen for convenience and partly because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose; the targeted two-laboratory reference disagreed on 2 of 7 duplicate samples; strip lots were not reported. The biases can run in either direction; very serious, two levels.

inconsistency.note: Both studies find etizolam poorly detected; the difference in degree (half of etizolam-only samples positive in programme data, never in pure solution) may reflect other reacting compounds, untargeted benzodiazepines or lots, and is reported, not rated.

indirectness.note: Staff-read strips at harm-reduction sites in one urban area (2018 to 2020) and pure solutions in a laboratory; one brand, made for urine.

imprecision.note: 24 confirmed positives (interval 43 to 79 in 100) and 16 etizolam-only samples.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources; laboratory evaluations of test strips are not registered.

grade.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence starts high; Laing et al.'s agreement figures are accuracy evidence with high risk of bias (METHODS §6.3; brief), so two levels for risk of bias and one each for indirectness and imprecision take it to the floor of very low. Rated as worded. Status replicated: independent teams (British Columbia; NIST) both found etizolam poorly detected; Sisco et al. (2024b) is filed in-vitro.
